title: A Warning for the Swayamvara
story:
The kings of the earth were gathered in the golden assembly hall of Bhishmaka at Kundina, come for the swayamvara of the king's daughter, and when Krishna arrived with Garuda and the Yadavas at his back, the brightness of the gathering dimmed. The leading kings, well-read in the science of polity and expert in counsel, exchanged glances and fell silent, stricken with an anxiety they could not quite name.

Jarasandha rose to speak, and the hall attended as the gods attend the king of gods.

He began quietly, with a warning dressed as counsel. This Krishna who has come to Kundina, he said, is the well-known son of Vasudeva, endued with great energy and prowess. He has come for the maiden, and forsooth he will set forth mighty exertions to win her. You should behave according to the rules of polity, weighing your own strength and weakness.

Then his voice changed, and the kings heard what he really thought.

You know well what these two sons of Vasudeva did on Mount Gomanta, without Garuda's help. I cannot say how Krishna will fight now that the mighty car-warriors of the Yadava, Bhoja and Andhaka races stand with him. But when Vishnu sits on Garuda and sets forth his exertions for the maiden, even Indra, assisted by all the celestials, will not be able to stand in the battle-field.

And then, to the kings who had come to choose a husband for a princess, Jarasandha began to recite what this suitor had been. When the universe lay under one all-spreading ocean, Vishnu took the form of a boar, raised the drowned earth from the nether region, and killed the Daitya king Hiranyaksha. The unconquerable Hiranyakashipu, who had not met his death in the three worlds, in sky or earth or nether region, in day or night, by anything dry or wet, was slain by Hari in his man-lion form. He bound the mighty Bali, foremost of Asuras, with a noose of promise, and sent him down to the nether region as a dwarf. At the junction of the ages he took birth in disguise from Jamadagni and Renuka as Rama with the axe, and cut down the thousand-armed Kartavirya, elated with the pride of his kingdom. He was Dasharatha's son Rama, born in the race of Ikshvaku, who killed Ravana, the conqueror of the three worlds. In the war whose root was Taraka, eight-armed and seated on Garuda, he killed the Asuras who were elated with their boons, and with his discus, effulgent like the sun, he killed the demon Kalanemi who terrorized the gods.

The hall was very still now. And nearer still, Jarasandha went on. As a boy in the forest he slew the demons Dhenuka, Arishta and Pralamba. In his cowherd form, Devaki's son sported there and slew Putana, Keshi, the elephant Kuvalayapida, the wrestlers Chanura and Mushtika, and Kamsa with all his followers. In disguise he performed these superhuman feats.

"This is my sure understanding," Jarasandha said, "and I acquired it at Mathura. I consider Devaki's son Keshava the first cause of the celestials, the destroyer of the Asuras, Narayana, the ancient Purusha, the prime cause of the universe, Truth, the creator of all creatures manifest and unmanifest, unconquerable, unborn, eternal, the lord of the three worlds. Can Garuda be the carrier of a mere man, even a mortal lord paramount? When Janarddana displays his prowess for the maiden, what powerful man will be able to stand before Garuda? Forsooth I tell you that Vishnu himself has come for this swayamvara. Mighty is the calamity that will befall you on his arrival here. Do whatever you think proper after this."

He sat down, and for a long moment no one moved. Then Sunitha rose and gave his voice to the king of Magadha's words, and the kings knew that the warning would not be argued away.

Outside the golden hall the evening drew in, and in the city of Kundina the lamps were being lit for a festival that suddenly felt less like a festival. The kings sat on among the variegated coverings of their seats, each man alone with the name Jarasandha had spoken aloud in council, the name none of them had wanted to say and none of them could now forget.
reflection: It is Jarasandha, Krishna's declared enemy and the man who had bound the kings into war against him, who names Krishna plainly before the assembled princes: not a rival suitor but Vishnu himself. Hatred here produces a clarity the indifferent kings do not share; the enemy sees exactly whom he is fighting, even as he resolves to fight him anyway.
next_story_tease: But the kings did not answer with one voice, for Dantavakra would speak for peace and Salwa for war.
hero_scene: In Bhishmaka's golden assembly hall at Kundina, Jarasandha stands among the seated kings, one hand raised, speaking with heavy certainty, while the assembled monarchs lean forward in alarm beneath the hall's lamps.

the lamps of the evening city beyond
